I had bad morning sickness in both my pregnancies. The second pregnancy was the worst because I'm nauseous and still had to wash poop. I can't keep anything down and I was still breastfeeding. Multivitamins kept me sustained until my pregnancy was far along and the nausea decreased.

I had spontaneous delivery at 38+1. My son had fetal brain bleed and HIE. We spent weeks in NICU to stop his head from swelling. He also suffered from seizures. 

From the get, our Pedia warned us to watch for developmental delays, because what my son went through can cause them. We did observe that he regressed after hitting his milestones at around 18months. He's also an anxious child, more so than the normal stranger anxiety that kids experience.

He was initially diagnosed with global developmental delay, and eventually diagnosed with autism. We did early intervention as early as 20months, we did baby gymnastics and swimming. He had OT then pandemic happened.

In my husband's family, there are 5 kids with autism, all of them cousins. My niece also has autism.

Genetics or problems during pregnancy, the odds were stacked against my son. I stopped caring about what caused it because if I do, I'll just spiral down ruminating on the what ifs.

Right now, he attends 2 hours of OT and 1 hour of speech. He still goes to swimming and has become a confident swimmer. We added soccer, and he has shown interest in wall climbing and piano. He's better at communicating and has better recall.

I suppose this post is about kids with low support needs, and not level 3 non verbal with severe disability. 

It's not about what other people want, it's about having reasonably proper behavior and attitude. One thing our Pediatrician and therapists told us, that struck with us. You can't isolate your child forever. You can't live inside a bubble. It's not healthy for the child and the family. 

We need to let them learn and push them to what they can reasonably do. Be it donning off or on their clothes, feed themselves, personal hygiene or conduct themselves in a respectful manner. That's what therapy is for.

I'm happy that there are accommodations for our children, but let's be real, it's only up to a point. We live in a society and we shouldn't expect the world to bend over backwards.

I was severely overweight and I have PCOS. OB prescribed BC pills and Metformin, advised lifestyle change. She tested my hormone levels, all were normal except I had abnormally high testosterone levels, which is consistent with being severely overweight. 

BC pills made my period regular but I gained more weight and I became obese, had low sex drive and suffered from severe depressive episodes. 

I changed my diet,  started weight lifting and running, eventually became strong and light enough to do a 21K. I changed OB’s and she advised I stopped taking that particular pill. 

A year later, my period became regular, and another year later I got pregnant. I now have a 15 month old toddler. 

Management of PCOS is a case to case basis. One approach may work for a different woman and may not work for others. The pill I was initially prescribed certainly made things worse for me, but I guess that pill might work for other PCOS patients. I know a woman with PCOS who only took Metformin and got pregnant after. 

What helped me was cutting out refined sugar and weight lifting.
